title: The calendar, again
tomorrow: what's a shepherd with a flute doing on a big book's cover?

cards: Open the calendar on your phone and it's full of birthdays you forgot you saved. The Church's calendar is fuller still. Its book of saints, the Roman Martyrology, names someone to remember on every day of the year.
So is that too much, or exactly right? Inside the Church, there are two honest answers, and each one has a real case.

teach.b: One side says: Christ's own story comes first.
The Second Vatican Council asked that the feasts of the saints not take the place of the feasts that celebrate salvation itself: Christmas, Easter, the Sundays and the seasons.
It suggested that many saints be kept by a single country, diocese or religious order, rather than by the whole Church. So the calendar for everyone was trimmed.
On this view, a year packed with saints can bury the story they all point to.

teach.h: THE OTHER: EVERY DAY, A FACE.
teach.b: The other side says: every day, someone. The Martyrology is still read, day by day, in many monasteries.
Families keep name days, parishes keep their patrons, and a teenager can find the saint born in her own century on her own birthday.

The Catechism says that when the Church remembers the martyrs and saints, it proclaims the paschal mystery in them: Christ's death and rising, lived out in a person. On this view, the saints don't crowd the story.

They are the story, told in face after face. Here's the one to tell a friend: the same council document that trimmed the calendar also says the feasts of the saints proclaim the wonderful works of Christ in his servants.

teach.h: BOTH WANT CHRIST AT THE CENTER.
teach.b: Both sides want Christ at the center.
The other finds him in a different face each morning. Scripture keeps a line for both: "All things have their season."

how: Catholics follow the liturgical year of seasons and Sundays, and keep memorials of saints through it; many monasteries read the day's entry from the Roman Martyrology, and families celebrate name days and patron saints.

games.q: your cousin loves knowing the saint for every day. your aunt says the seasons matter more. you side with your cousin. what's your aunt's best case?
o: the council asked that saints' days not crowd out Christ's own feasts.
the saints just matter less to the Church than they used to.
the old saints' calendar was full of mistakes, so it was dropped.
games.why: her case is in the Second Vatican Council's liturgy document. your cousin's is in the same document: the saints proclaim the wonderful works of Christ. both keep Christ at the center.

practice: Write tomorrow's date by hand on a scrap of paper, and leave a space beside it for a name.
If you already know a saint the Church remembers tomorrow, write the name in; if not, the blank is fine, a small question waiting for the morning.
